title: Nobody Changed Any Code, But Plan Is Broken
intro: CI plans passed yesterday. Today, with zero code changes, every plan fails with 'Unsupported argument' errors on S3 buckets.

steps.prompt: Check which provider versions this CI run actually installed.
steps.hint: Compare against what the project was using before.

steps.prompt: AWS provider 6.0.0 — a major version. Check the constraint that allowed it.
'>= 4.0' allows any future major version. Check whether the lock file that would have prevented this is in the repo.
steps.hint: The lock file records exact provider versions — but only if it's committed.

steps.prompt: The lock file is gitignored, so every CI run resolves the newest allowed version. After changing the constraint to '~> 5.0' in code, reinitialize to pick a compatible version.
steps.fake_output:
- Finding hashicorp/aws versions matching "~> 5.0"...
- Installing hashicorp/aws v5.68.0...
Terraform has created a lock file .terraform.lock.hcl
steps.hint: -upgrade is needed to move DOWN from 6.0.0 to the newest 5.x.

steps.fake_output: No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
steps.hint: Then remove .terraform.lock.hcl from .gitignore and commit it.

resolution: Two mistakes combined: a loose version constraint ('>= 4.0' permits any future major version, including breaking ones) and a gitignored .terraform.lock.hcl. Together they meant every CI run silently picked up the newest provider, and the day a major version with breaking changes shipped, every pipeline broke with no code change at all. The lock file exists precisely to make provider versions reproducible — it should always be committed (only the .terraform/ directory should be ignored). Pin providers with '~>' to a major version, commit the lock file, and upgrade deliberately in its own pull request, where the plan diff can be reviewed.
